title: How electrolyte properties and applied potential impact pathways and performance in electrochemical nitrate reduction
abstract: Electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction (NO 3 RR) is a promising route for the valorization of nitrate pollutants into ammonia; however, while extensive efforts have focused on catalyst development, the influence of electrolyte properties on NO 3 RR performance has been largely overlooked and remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the electrolyte alone contributes significantly and systematically to the reaction, independent of catalyst identity. To identify the electrocatalytic trends driven by the electrolyte, key parameters —including pH, nitrate concentration, and co-existing cations— were investigated through rationally designed electrochemical experiments performed across multiple metals (Cu, Ag, Pd, Au, Bi, Mo, and Ti), enabling differentiation of catalyst-specific behavior from electrolyte-driven effects. We find that pH and co-existing cations are critical, as they modulate interfacial proton availability, nitrate adsorption, intermediate stabilization, and controlled protonation toward ammonia formation. The effect of nitrate concentration depends on these two parameters as well as the applied potential. Importantly, our study highlights a commonly neglected aspect: alkali metal cations are not simple spectators but act as critical electrostatic field mediators in NO 3 RR. This work provides guidance for engineering electrolytes for nitrate-to-ammonia electrocatalytic systems and calls for redefining alkali metal cations as a key tuning parameter.

title: Insight into Zn, S dual vacancy-mediated electron redistribution: Enhancing piezo-photocatalytic H2O2 production and pollutant removal over carbonized spider chitin/ZnIn2S4
abstract: Exploring a photocatalytic route for the efficient production of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) from pure water, without the addition of extra sacrificial agents, remains a challenging research endeavor. To address the core bottlenecks of severe carrier recombination, weak piezoelectric response, and insufficient active sites in ZnIn2S4 (ZIS) based catalysts. This study fabricated carbonized chitin supports using natural spider cuticle as the precursor (TC), and in-situ constructed Zn and S dual vacancies (VZn/S) modified TC/ZIS-VZn/S composite piezoelectric photocatalytic system through a one-step solvothermal approach. The optimized TC/ZIS-VZn/S-2 exhibits a photocatalytic H2O2 production rate of up to 48.57 mM g-1 h-1 in the effluent. In systems integrating piezo-photocatalytic organic pollutant degradation with H2O2 synergistic production, this rate is enhanced by a factor of 2.1. This phenomenon arises from the disruption of the local lattice symmetry of ZIS by dual vacancies, which facilitates the formation of a local oriented electric field (LOEF) and enhances the directional charge transfer path of In-S-Zn. Meanwhile, ZIS introduces a considerable number of asymmetric dipoles within the unit cell, which significantly enhances the spontaneous polarization strength and piezoelectric performance of the material. This study uncovers the intrinsic mechanism by which VZn/S dual vacancies regulated local electron rearrangement enhances piezoelectric photocatalytic performance.

title: Interfacial ruthenium–titania nanosheet engineering for highly selective electrocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia across a wide pH range
abstract: Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction (NO₃RR) is a promising strategy for simultaneous wastewater remediation and decentralized ammonia production, but requires catalysts with high activity, NH₃ selectivity, and stability. Here, we report a Ru/TiNS electrocatalyst composed of well-dispersed Ru nanoparticles on oxygen-deficient monolayer titania nanosheets (TiNS), enabling simultaneous precise control over nitrate adsorption, interfacial charge transfer, and hydrogen evolution reaction. Systematic variation of Ru loading, support, and electrolyte establishes clear structure–activity relationships. The optimized 25%Ru–TiNS catalyst achieves 120 ± 4 mA·cm⁻² at 0 V vs. RHE in alkaline electrolyte, maintaining high NH₃ selectivity across a broad pH range. Its superior performance originates from the efficient generation and utilization of active hydrogen species (H*) via enhanced water dissociation on Ru sites, which are continuously consumed by nitrate-derived intermediates stabilized on TiNS. This kinetically matched hydrogen supply–consumption process enables high Faradaic efficiency over a wide potential range while suppressing competing hydrogen evolution. Operando Raman spectroscopy reveals enhanced nitrate adsorption and interfacial water activation under cathodic potentials, evidenced by increased nitrate-related Raman bands and changes in interfacial O–H structure. Complementary DFT calculations demonstrate strong metal–support interactions and electronic coupling at the Ru–TiNS interface, promoting nitrate activation and optimizing hydrogenation energetics. As a result, 25%Ru–TiNS outperforms Ru supported on reduced graphene oxide and carbon nanotubes in both activity and selectivity. In a paired NO₃RR/OER electrolyzer, the catalyst delivers 97% NH₃ Faradaic efficiency at 1.26 V, ∼0.3 V lower than conventional water electrolysis, highlighting its potential for energy-efficient ammonia production and wastewater treatment.

title: Unveiling carrier relaxation trajectories in π–d hybridized CoFe-PBA/polyaniline S-scheme heterojunctions for integrated solar-driven oxidation and distillation
abstract: S-scheme heterojunctions excel in solar-driven water treatment and energy conversion, yet interfacial carrier relaxation remains insufficiently understood, with little insight into their catalytic–photothermal trade-off. Here, we construct a π–d hybridized CoFe-based Prussian Blue Analogue/polyaniline heterostructure to regulate interfacial carrier behavior. Crystal field analysis reveals that π electrons from polyaniline selectively inject into Fe 3d orbitals, reconstructing interfacial electric fields. Upon photoexcitation, carriers in Co/Fe 3d orbitals undergo a characteristic interfacial relaxation process (τ 3 = 913.2 ps) involving transfer toward π* C–N orbitals, suppressing radiative recombination and enhancing nonradiative relaxation. This trajectory helps preserve high-redox-potential electrons and holes for catalysis, while enabling interfacial carrier nonradiative relaxation to contribute to localized heat generation, revealing a carrier-relaxation-mediated coupling between catalytic oxidation and photothermal conversion at S-scheme interfaces. A photothermal catalytic evaporator based on this mechanism demonstrates promising performance for simultaneous volatile organic compound removal and clean-water production, proposing a dual-function strategy for solar-driven oxidation–distillation.

title: Regulating hot-carrier dynamics via indium anchoring for highly stable CO2 photoreduction on CsPbBr3 nanocrystals
abstract: CsPbBr3 perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) demonstrate exceptional photocatalytic potential in CO2 conversion through superior light harvesting and multi-exciton generation. However, their practical application is fundamentally hindered by structural instability that compromises carrier utilization. This study, using femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy and temperature-dependent photoluminescence, reveals that dynamic coupling between hot carriers and lattice vibrations drives structural degradation via localized phonon excitations. To address this, we engineered indium (In)-anchored CsPbBr3 PNCs by targeted modification of surface Pb centers. The In-anchoring passivates defect-associated empty p-orbitals while prolonging the hot carrier lifetime by 98.86%. Furthermore, the introduced In atoms induce electronic localization, which suppresses phonon-driven lattice vibrations. As a result, charge separation and transport are dramatically enhanced, leading to a significant improvement in both CO2 reduction activity and stability. In contrast to CsPbBr3 PNCs, which completely deactivate within 20 h, In-anchored CsPbBr3 PNCs maintain stability over long-term operation for up to 60 h, while simultaneously exhibiting a 14.85-fold enhancement in CO yield. This study establishes a fundamental strategy for stabilizing perovskite photocatalysts by regulating hot carrier-lattice interactions, offering new insights into the design of high-performance CO2 reduction systems.

title: Boosting the alkaline hydrogen evolution performance of nickel nanoparticles by engineering frustrated Lewis pair for industrial water splitting electrolyzers
abstract: Efficient alkaline HER electrocatalysis demands simultaneous optimization of water dissociation, hydrogen adsorption/desorption, and hydroxide release for fast kinetics. Herein, we introduce a scalable, one-pot pyrolysis method enabling large-area electrode fabrication (up to 50 × 50 cm2) that produces a highly active catalyst: uniformly dispersed Ni nanoparticles anchored on low-crystallinity, oxygen-vacancy (Ov)-rich MoO2-x directly grown on nickel foam (Ni-LC-MoO2-x /NF). The complementary interaction between Ov (Lewis acidic sites) and Ni (mild Lewis basic sites) markedly enhances performance. The optimized catalyst exhibits superior areal activity and exceptional durability at industrial current densities, outperforming most state-of-the-art non-precious electrocatalysts. In situ spectroscopy and DFT calculations reveal the mechanism: Ov promotes H2O adsorption and rapid H-OH cleavage, while Ni facilitates efficient H2 release, collectively lowering energy barriers. Deployed as the cathode in a practical AWE electrolyzer (80 °C, 30 wt% KOH), it sustains stable operation at 0.8 A cm-2 for over 1600 hours with negligible degradation.

title: Clusters induced electron redistribution of single-atom Co sites in freestanding nanofiber electrodes for efficient Zn-Air batteries
abstract: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) at the air cathode of zinc-air batteries (ZABs) involves a multi-step proton‑coupled electron transfer, yet its sluggish kinetics severely limit energy conversion efficiency. While the single‑atom–cluster synergy enhances ORR activity, a deep clarifying its dynamic mechanism and integrating powder catalysts into practical devices remain challenging. Herein, we fabricate a freestanding nanofiber electrode comprising cobalt single atoms and sub‑nanometric cobalt clusters via electrospinning (CoSA/AC‑N‑PCNFs). Theoretical calculations show that adjacent Co clusters modulate the electronic structure of Co‑N4 sites to enhance electron filling in the σ* orbital (Co 3dz²–O 2pz hybridization), which promotes OH* desorption and optimizes the d‑band structure, thereby significantly improving the ORR activity. Focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy and electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the nanofiber electrode exhibits a 2.1‑fold increase in the relative diffusion coefficient, which not only maximizes the exposure of active sites but also provides efficient pathways for gas/electron transport. Resultingly, the CoSA/AC‑N‑PCNFs electrode delivers a half‑wave potential of 0.923 V and a negligible H2O2 yield. This electrode enabled ZABs to deliver a high power density of 300 mW cm-2 along with excellent durability exceeding 500 h. Furthermore, the CoSA/AC-N-PCNFs exhibit promising potential for use in flexible ZABs.

title: Strain-induced local polarization field modulation and spin state alternation in atomic Ni-anchored carbon nitride for boosting piezo-photocatalysis
abstract: Piezo-photocatalysis enables solar-to-chemical conversion driven by both light and mechanical energy, yet its practical efficiency is hampered by two inherent obstacles: piezopotential shielding from excessive charge accumulation at polar edges, and spatiotemporal mismatch between dynamic carrier migration and surface catalytic sites. Herein, a series of nNi-CN piezo-photocatalysts with tunable single-atom Ni loading was synthesized via post-impregnation to tackle this critical limitation. Ni single atoms are anchored in the triangular planar cavities of carbon nitride (CN) with a well-defined Ni-N 6 coordination. The embedded Ni not only enhances the in-plane dipole moment and piezoelectric response of CN, but also induces radial local polarization fields centered at Ni sites, which redirect carrier migration pathways, shorten carrier diffusion distance, and effectively suppress piezopotential shielding by confining carriers at local active centers. More importantly, strain exerts a dual regulatory role in synchronously modulating the local polarization field intensity and the spin-state alternation of Ni sites under different strain regions. Compressive strain optimizes the Ni spin state toward a thermodynamically favorable hydrogen evolution configuration, enabling spatial alignment between electron accumulation terminals and reduction active sites and realizing dynamic spatiotemporal matching of charge supply and active-site utilization. The optimized 2Ni-CN exhibits exceptional piezo-photocatalytic water splitting performance under ultrasonic (40 kHz, 100 W) and LED illumination (36 W), achieving a H 2 production rate of 440.7 μmol·h -1 ·g -1 (23.6 times that of pristine CN) with a synergistic enhancement factor of 2.27. This study puts forward a versatile single-atom engineering strategy to suppress piezopotential shielding and resolve carrier-site spatiotemporal mismatch, paving an innovative pathway toward high-efficiency piezo-photocatalysts.

title: Cathode-separator synergy unlocks ultralow self-discharge and shuttle-free high loading zinc-iodine batteries
abstract: The practical application of aqueous zinc-iodine batteries (AZIBs) remains hindered by sluggish iodine redox kinetics, severe shuttle effects from irreversible polyiodide byproducts, and dendrite formation and corrosion at the Zn anode. Herein, we introduce a cathode-separator synergy strategy, which integrates the porous carbon cathode physical confines iodine, while the NiS 2 -modified separator provides strong chemisorption and catalytic conversion of iodine species. Benefiting from this coupling effect, the Zn//NiS 2 @GF//PC/I 2 battery delivers a superior rate capability of 334.2 mAh g −1 at 0.2 A g −1 , remains above 1.31 V within 464 h with an ultralow self-discharge rate of 0.000625 V h −1 , and an outstanding lifespan exceeding 7500 cycles with ∼100% average Coulombic efficiency. Moreover, a pouch cell with high iodine loading of 6.0 mg cm −2 likewise demonstrates excellent cycling stability of 167.0 mAh g −1 at 0.3 A g −1 . Notably, these performances exhibit exceptional competitiveness among AZIBs with modified separator systems. Comprehensive ex-situ Raman/XPS analysis and detailed DFT theoretical calculations reveal that the coupled adsorption-catalysis mechanism reduces the adsorption energy and conversion energy barrier of iodine species, while simultaneously accelerating the conversion of polyiodide and suppressing side reactions at the Zn anode, thereby achieving ultralow self-discharge and shuttling-free behavior. Note that in-situ EIS and DRT electrochemical tests were innovatively used to reveal the charge transfer mechanism at the cathode-separator interface, further supporting the reversibility of iodine redox. This work provides mechanism insights and universal modification strategies for advancing AZIBs, significantly promoting the further development of aqueous zinc iodine energy technology for practical applications.

title: Suppressing CO formation in low-temperature methanol steam reforming via Ce-modified CuZnGa layered oxide catalysts
abstract: Cu-based layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are widely recognized as effective catalysts for low-temperature methanol steam reforming, yet achieving high hydrogen productivity together with near-complete suppression of CO formation remains challenging. Here, we report the synthesis and evaluation of a series of CuZnGa LDH-derived catalysts and Ce-modified analogues prepared via an aqueous miscible organic method, which enables high metal dispersion and precise structural control. The optimized CuZnGa catalyst exhibits a hydrogen production rate of 16.9 µmol H 2 ·g cat −1 ·s −1 at 180 °C with an H 2 /CO ratio exceeding 3500, outperforming many state-of-the-art low-temperature systems. Importantly, the incorporation of small amounts of Ce further suppresses CO formation while maintaining high hydrogen productivity. Combined spectroscopic characterization and density functional theory calculations reveal that Ce is incorporated into the LDH lattice by substituting Ga 3+ sites up to a critical threshold, beyond which highly dispersed CeO x species are formed. These species provide mobile lattice oxygen that participates in a Mars-van Krevelen-type pathway, selectively oxidizing CO and suppressing the reverse water-gas shift reaction. This study establishes a clear relationship between Ce speciation, oxygen mobility, and catalytic selectivity in LDH-derived systems. The resulting catalysts demonstrate the potential of interface-engineered Cu-based materials for efficient low-temperature hydrogen production with minimal CO contamination.

title: Performance enhancement of Pd-based selective ammonia oxidation catalysts through forced dynamic operation
abstract: In light of the increasing relevance of alternative energy carriers, the established domain of emission control is confronted with novel challenges. Among these carriers, ammonia (NH 3 ) has emerged as particularly promising due to its high energy density and carbon-free nature. This study focuses on the selective catalytic oxidation (SCO) of NH 3 to elemental nitrogen (N 2 ) under lean conditions. While conventional platinum-based catalysts exhibit high activity, they suffer from poor N 2 selectivity and significant formation of nitrous oxide (N 2 O), a potent greenhouse gas. As an alternative, palladium-based catalysts are investigated due to their inherently higher selectivity toward N 2 . Although palladium exhibits limited activity under static feed conditions, its performance is markedly enhanced under forced dynamic operation (FDO), wherein short, intermittent reducing pulses are introduced through oxygen cut-off. This operational mode not only boosts catalytic activity beyond that of platinum but also preserves palladium’s superior selectivity. Operando time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and ex situ Raman spectroscopic analysis of spent catalyst samples indicate that FDO promotes the formation of metallic palladium, which exhibits higher activity compared to palladium oxide that is the predominant phase under lean conditions. Operando XAS uncovers that a finite fraction of metallic palladium is retained at the catalyst inlet, enhancing low-temperature activity and likely contributing to improved long-term stability as long as 300 °C is not exceeded for extended periods. These findings correspond directly to axially resolved concentration profiles of gas phase species, which reveal the development of a highly active front zone during FDO, where the majority of NH 3 conversion occurs selectively to N 2 . This phenomenon is observed under both dry and humid conditions, underscoring the robustness of the approach. The results suggest that FDO enables the use of significantly shorter monolithic converters for selective NH 3 oxidation, i.e., a reduction of length by up to 50% in realistic humid conditions, thereby offering substantial reductions in both reactor volume and noble metal demand for practical applications.

title: Promotion of CO2-to-formate conversion via fluorine modification on amorphous indium hydroxides
abstract: Amorphous catalysts feature highly defective structures, providing more potential active species for electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR). However, uncontrollable amorphous catalysts often lead to excessive side reactions and unforeseen structural reconstruction, largely suppressing the electroactivity. This study builds upon our earlier strategy relative to fluorine erosion, further elucidating an electrochemically-driven fluorine-erosion mechanism. Specifically, reactive fluorine species generated via the reversible electroreduction of polytetrafluoroethylene from the gas diffusion layer can effectively fluorinate amorphous indium hydroxides under CO2RR conditions, thereby creating active indium-fluorine content. This process enables the indium species to maintain a high valence state under electroreduction. Theoretical calculations demonstrate that fluorine-induced indium species facilitate CO2 adsorption, promoting CO2RR pathway and subsequent formate production. The enhanced CO2RR performance can reach an impressive Faradaic efficiency of 93% at the partial current density of 648 mA cm-2 toward formate. This work sheds light on a novel approach for the structural control and modification for amorphous catalysts, highlighting a novel mechanism for fluorine erosion from the gas diffusion layer during electrocatalysis.

title: Uncovering CO2-driven selective oxidation of HCN to N2 over Pt/Al2O3 during the gasification-regeneration of FCC catalysts
abstract: Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is a hazardous nitrogenous pollutant formed during fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) catalyst regeneration, yet its mitigation under oxygen-lean, CO 2 -rich regeneration environments remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate for the first time that Pt/Al 2 O 3 catalysts enable a deep oxidation of HCN to N 2 by CO 2 , a pathway fundamentally distinct from O 2 -assisted HCN oxidation that leads to the formation of the secondary pollutant, NO x . Using industrial spent FCC catalysts as a case study, Pt/Al 2 O 3 was found to simultaneously promote the CO 2 -gasification of coke and reduce HCN emissions, overcoming the intrinsically slow kinetics of CO 2 -mediated HCN oxidation. Furthermore, through the implementation of a two-stage CO 2 and O 2 regeneration strategy, the emission of HCN was completely suppressed and the total NO emissions were reduced by ~76-92% compared with conventional air-fired regeneration, while preserving the physicochemical integrity of the regenerated catalyst. HCN oxidation experiments, XAS characterization, and DFT free-energy calculations together reveal that metallic Pt sites mediate a Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism in which HCN undergoes dissociative adsorption to form adsorbed H and CN species, followed by thermodynamically favorable coupling of CN* with weakly adsorbed CO 2 to form NCO* and CO. Subsequently, NCO* decomposes to N*, which recombines to yield N 2 . This work reveals a previously unrecognized catalytic function of Pt/Al 2 O 3 that enables simultaneous control of HCN and NO x emissions in a low-carbon FCC regeneration strategy.

title: Unlocking industrial OER performance via corrosion-induced interface engineering and built-in electric fields
abstract: Developing oxygen evolution electrocatalysts that combine fast kinetics, structural robustness, and scalability under industrially relevant alkaline conditions remains a major challenge. Herein, we report a corrosion-induced strategy to in situ construct a NiFe-LDH@Ni(OH)2 heterointerfacial electrode on nickel foam. The Fermi-level mismatch between NiFe-LDH and Ni(OH)2 generates a built-in electric field, inducing interfacial charge redistribution and facilitating catalyst reconstruction during OER. Combined spectroscopic, electrochemical, and theoretical analyses suggest that the interfacial electric field promotes directional electron transfer, accelerates the formation of active NiOOH/NiFeOOH species, and optimizes intermediate adsorption. As a result, the electrode delivers 100 mA·cm-2 at an overpotential of 240 mV in 1 M KOH, with a Tafel slope of 30.5 mV·dec-1. Under industrially relevant conditions (80 ℃, 30 wt% KOH), it achieves 0.5 and 1.0 A·cm-2 at 1.76 and 1.93 V, respectively, in an AEM electrolyzer, with low energy consumption (4.64 kWh/Nm3 H2) and stable operation. This work highlights corrosion-induced heterointerface engineering as an effective strategy to couple interfacial electric-field regulation with active-phase evolution for alkaline oxygen evolution reaction.

title: Interfacial Ni³⁺ oxyhydroxide stabilization enables selective high-current-density ethanol oxidation in AEM electrolysis
abstract: Substituting the anodic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) with ethanol oxidation offers a promising route to lower the energy consumption of anion-exchange-membrane (AEM) electrolysis, but selective oxidation at industrially relevant current densities is often undermined by the emergence of OER-active states. Here, we identify stabilized Ni³⁺ oxyhydroxide as the key state that redirects anodic Ni chemistry away from oxygen evolution and toward selective ethanol oxidation under high-current operation. On a metallic Ni/defect-rich NiO heterointerface, anodic polarization triggers surface hydroxylation while retaining strong electronic coupling across the interface. Mechanistic studies combining operando Raman spectroscopy, post-reaction TEM/XPS, and density functional theory reveal that interfacial charge transfer facilitates early Ni²⁺/Ni³⁺ conversion, stabilizes Ni³⁺ oxyhydroxide species, decreases the OH* deprotonation barrier, and inhibits overoxidation toward OER. This mechanism delivers 100 mA cm⁻² at only 120 mV and preserves selective, bubble-free ethanol oxidation up to 900 mA cm⁻². In an ethanol-hybrid AEM electrolyzer, the corresponding anode lowers the cell voltage by 370 mV at 1.0 A cm⁻² compared with conventional water electrolysis and sustains stable electrolysis for 200 h at 0.5 A cm⁻². Our results establish Ni³⁺ oxyhydroxide stabilization as a general design principle for high-rate selective anodic oxidation and energy-efficient hydrogen production.

title: Understanding the Roles of Cu and ZnO in Electrochemical CO2-Nitrate Coupling toward C-N Product Formation
abstract: Electrochemical co‑reduction of CO 2 and nitrate offers a sustainable route to C-N compounds but is limited by competing reactions and unclear mechanisms. Cu-Zn catalysts have been widely studied, the specific roles of Cu and ZnO remain unresolved toward the first C-N formation. Here, this work studies how Cu dispersion, particle size, and Zn and Cu interactions can influence C-N formation by tuning calcination temperature. Results showed that larger ZnO particles formed at a high calcination temperature exhibited higher formaldoxime productivity (96.5 µg·h⁻¹·mg⁻¹ cat ) showing ZnO as active catalyst towards formaldoxime while Cu addition suppressed C-N formation and promoted H 2 and NH 4 + generation. A validated analytical framework combining HPLC and ¹H NMR was developed, where proton exchangeability and metal coordination tests supported the assignment of metal‑associated formaldoxime. Post-electrolysis thin-film X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy revealed partial surface reconstruction despite the overall structural stability of Cu-ZnO/700 observed by in situ Synchrotron XRD, highlighting the dynamic roles of Cu and Zn species during co-reduction. The results also supported that ZnO, rather than Cu, promoted metal-formaldoxime via *HCO and *NOH key intermediates under N-rich conditions, as evidenced by in situ Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with control experiments. Density Functional Theory calculations proposed the conversion of CO 2 to *HCO as the overall rate-determining step toward C-N coupling. These findings highlight the importance of catalyst design, where tuning ZnO particle size and limiting Cu dispersion modulates the balance of carbon‑ and nitrogen‑derived species, offering a pathway to improved formaldoxime performance in electrochemical CO 2 and nitrate conversion.

title: Structural and functional tuning of carbon-supported NiMo hydrogen evolution reaction electrocatalysts for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis
abstract: s NiMo/C electrocatalyst (EC) can be a promising alternative to scarce and overpriced platinum group metals (PGMs) for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs). However, resolving the optimal Ni-to-Mo ratio and understanding how the carbon support helps develop a suitable electrocatalytic architecture remain unclear. Therefore, two EC series with varying Ni-to-Mo ratios, supported over two different carbon substrates, i.e., Vulcan and Ketjenblack (KJB), were developed and thoroughly investigated. Structural characterizations via X-ray diffraction and X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) highlighted that initially the Mo tended to substitute within the host nickel’s FCC lattice; however, increasing the Mo content led to the enhanced formation of bulk oxide phases, whereas different morphological makeovers were observed for both Vulcan- and KJB-based samples through the scanning transmission electron microscope. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicated the highest Ni 2+ /Ni 0 ratio in Ni70Mo30/KJB; however, in both sample series, further increasing the Mo content led to a progressive enrichment of surface MoO₃, causing decay of HER performance. In the same samples, operando XAS specified beneficial Mo dissolution-redeposition while maintaining the Ni sites, primarily in a metallic state during HER, with limited and reversible hydroxide formation predominantly in the electrochemically active α-Ni(OH) 2 in the HER regime. The highest half-cell HER activity was achieved at a Ni: Mo ratio of 70:30, particularly with Ni70Mo30/KJB requiring an overpotential of only 119.6 mV. Eventually, when tested in AEMWE operating at 80 ºC with a NiFe 2 O 4 anode, it realized a current density of 3.82 A cm -2 at 2.2 V along with excellent operational durability.

title: Stability of Co, Ni, and Fe in CoNiFeP electrocatalyst during hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions in alkaline media
abstract: Transition-metal phosphide catalysts show high activity for alkaline water splitting, but their stability remains underexplored. Herein, the activity-stability relationship of an electrodeposited Co-Ni-Fe-P alloy for hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions (HER and OER) is investigated. At open-circuit potential (OCP), selective Co dissolution occurs, which is proportional to the KOH concentration and depends on the composition of the purge gas. Controlled H 2 and O 2 purging suppresses Co dissolution relative to Ar, indicating a strong coupling between electrode environment and Co stability. Furthermore, accelerated stress tests simulating electrolyzer start-up/shut-down reveal reaction-dependent dissolution dynamics. During HER, the dissolved Co at OCP decreases under cathodic cycling, indicating net removal of this species from the electrolyte, while Ni and Fe remain stable. Conversely, during OER, Co dissolution rate decreases markedly, revealing a stability trend of Fe < Ni < Co. This study highlights the critical need for protocols that simulate operational transients, offering new insights for designing durable water-splitting electrocatalysts.
